lessons.title: Creation, Evolution and the Sanctity of Human Life

before.content_html:
In the Beginning: The Catholic Understanding of Creation

The Catholic Church teaches that God is the ultimate source of all that exists. This is not simply the view that God ‘designed’ the universe like an architect working with existing materials — rather, Catholic theology holds that God created everything ex nihilo, meaning ‘out of nothing.’ This teaching goes back to the early Church, and the theologian Augustine of Hippo gave it precise formulation in his Confessions XII, 7, where he reasoned that if God made everything, he could not have needed any pre-existing material to work with. The very fact that something exists rather than nothing is entirely a gift of God.

Creation ex nihilo has two important consequences. First, it means the universe is entirely dependent on God: without God’s ongoing creative will, nothing would exist at all. Second, it means creation is fundamentally good — not a mistake or a prison for the soul, as some ancient philosophies taught, but a loving gift from a God whose goodness overflows into existence.

Two Genesis Accounts

The Bible opens with two distinct accounts of creation. The first, Genesis 1:1–2:3, is a structured, poetic account in which God creates over six days and rests on the seventh, declaring each stage ‘good’. The climax is the creation of humans in God’s imago Dei — in the image of God — as male and female. The second account, Genesis 2:4–24, is more personal and narrative in style: God forms the human being from the dust of the ground, breathes life into him, plants a garden, and forms a companion from his side.

The Catholic Church does not require a literal, seven-day reading of Genesis. Instead, the Church distinguishes between the religious truth these accounts communicate — that God is creator, humans are special, creation is good — and the question of how God brought creation about. This allows Catholic teaching to be open to scientific accounts of the universe’s origins while insisting that science and faith address different questions: science asks ‘how?’, theology asks ‘why?’ and ‘who?’

Key Fact

Genesis 1:1–2:3 gives a structured, six-day account emphasising God’s power and the goodness of creation. Genesis 2:4–24 gives a more personal account focusing on the human relationship with God and the earth. The Catholic Church reads both as conveying religious truth rather than scientific description.

Evolution: Science, Faith and Pope John Paul II

Charles Darwin’s work on natural selection proposed that species, including human beings, developed through gradual evolutionary processes over vast periods of time. Richard Dawkins, a contemporary evolutionary biologist, has argued from this that evolution is a ‘blind’ process with no direction or purpose — making the idea of a creator God unnecessary. This is sometimes called the ‘blind evolution’ view.

The Catholic Church’s position is more nuanced. In his 1996 Message to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences on the subject of evolution, Pope John Paul II stated (in paragraphs 3 and 4) that the theory of evolution is ‘more than a hypothesis’ given the convergence of evidence across multiple scientific fields, and that the Church can accept biological evolution as the means by which God brought about human life. However, he insisted that the spiritual dimension of the human person — the soul — is not the product of evolutionary processes but is directly created by God. This is sometimes called ‘theistic evolution’ or ‘planned evolution’: evolution is real, but it is God’s method, not a godless accident.

Catholic teaching holds that God is transcendent — utterly beyond and above the created order. God is not a being within the universe who can be observed by science; God is the ground of being on which everything else depends. This is why science and faith do not simply contradict each other: they operate at different levels of enquiry. Augustine’s insight in Confessions XII, 7, was that God must be the cause of all being, not a being among others. God’s omnipotence is not simply brute force but the power to bring existence itself into being from nothing.

The mystic Catherine of Siena, writing in her Dialogue (also known as the Dialogue of Divine Providence), expressed through a series of contemplative conversations with God that the soul’s deepest longing is for its creator, and that human dignity comes from the fact that God has made each soul in his own image. Catherine describes God as the source of all goodness and the soul as incomplete without its return to God — an insight that connects creation theology to ethics: if humans are made in God’s image, the way they are treated matters profoundly.

The Sanctity of Human Life

Catholic teaching holds that because human beings are made in the image of God, every human life has an intrinsic worth that cannot be measured in terms of usefulness, productivity or capacity. This is called the sanctity of human life. The principle is absolute: it applies from fertilisation to natural death, which is why the Catholic Church opposes both abortion and euthanasia.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church, at paragraph 2270, states that human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception. On euthanasia, Pope John Paul II’s encyclical Evangelium Vitae (1995), at paragraph 65, describes the intentional killing of a suffering person as gravely wrong — a violation of God’s sovereignty over life and death. The Church supports palliative care (relieving pain without hastening death) as an alternative to assisted dying.

Abortion is currently legal in Great Britain (up to 24 weeks under the Abortion Act 1967, as amended) and Catholic organisations such as the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children (SPUC) and local ‘Choose Life’ groups campaign against it. The Catholic Church regards the embryo as a human person from fertilisation, so abortion at any stage is considered a gravely serious act. The Catechism (paragraph 2270) is clear that the life of the unborn person must be protected absolutely.

The Catholic Church also takes a strong position on stewardship and protecting the planet, recognising that care for creation flows from the same theology that grounds human dignity. Pope Francis’ encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015), at paragraph 49, calls on Catholics to hear ‘both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor’, linking environmental responsibility to Catholic social teaching.

Non-Religious Views: Humanist and Secular Challenges

Non-religious thinkers approach the questions of creation and human life very differently. Stephen Hawking argued that the laws of physics can explain the universe’s origin without invoking a creator, pointing to the Big Bang as a natural event not requiring divine action. Richard Dawkins argues that ‘blind’ evolution — driven by natural selection with no purpose or direction — makes the idea of a creator God unnecessary.

On the value of human life, the philosopher Peter Singer has challenged what he calls speciesism — the idea that human beings automatically deserve more protection than other sentient creatures simply because they are human. Singer argues that what matters morally is an organism’s capacity to feel pain and have interests, not whether it belongs to the human species. This leads him to conclude that in some circumstances, the life of a non-human animal with a rich conscious life may be more morally valuable than the life of a severely brain-damaged human infant.

The ‘quality of life’ argument, used by organisations such as Dignity in Dying (which advocates for assisted dying) and by those who support a right to choose regarding abortion, holds that what matters is not simply being alive but whether life is experienced as meaningful or involves excessive suffering. This contrasts sharply with the Catholic ‘sanctity of life’ position, which holds that life’s value is intrinsic rather than dependent on the person’s condition.

Key Fact

Peter Singer’s concept of ‘speciesism’ challenges the idea that human life is automatically more valuable than animal life. Catholics respond that the imago Dei gives human beings a unique dignity that goes beyond mere sentience or capacity for suffering.
before.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark ‘explain two beliefs’ questions on this topic, examiners award marks for precise Catholic sources: Catechism 2270, Evangelium Vitae 65, Augustine’s Confessions XII,7. Name the document, give the paragraph or book/chapter reference, then explain what it actually teaches — never just name it. For 15-mark evaluation questions, contrast the Catholic ‘sanctity of life’ position with the Humanist ‘quality of life’ position, include Peter Singer’s speciesism critique, and reach a clear personal conclusion. Remember that spelling, punctuation and grammar carry marks on 15-mark questions — write in full sentences throughout.

lessons.title: Scripture, Sacred Art and Catholic Symbolism

before.content_html:
Revelation and Inspiration

Catholics believe God has communicated with humanity — this communication is called revelation. Revelation takes two main forms. Natural revelation is the knowledge of God that can be reached through reason and the observation of creation — the world itself points to its Creator. Special revelation is God’s direct communication through historical events, the prophets and supremely through Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh.

The Bible is the product of divine inspiration. Catholic teaching holds that God is the principal author of Scripture, working through human authors. This means the Bible is truly the Word of God, and yet also truly a human document — written in particular languages, by particular people, in particular historical and cultural contexts. The Second Vatican Council’s document Dei Verbum teaches that to understand what God intends to communicate, the reader must pay attention to what the human authors were actually saying and the literary forms they used.

Key Fact

Catholic teaching holds that Scripture is both fully divine (God is its ultimate author) and fully human (written by people in specific times and cultures). To interpret Scripture correctly, the reader must understand the literary form being used — whether the text is history, poetry, law, parable, prophecy or another genre.

Literary Forms in Genesis

The opening chapters of Genesis have been a source of rich debate. Catholics do not require a literal reading of Genesis 1–2 as a scientific account of origins. The Catechism of the Catholic Church and the teaching of Dei Verbum encourage attention to literary form. Genesis 1 has the structure of a liturgical poem — a rhythmic seven-day framework with refrains. Genesis 2 is a different account, more narrative in style, focusing on the garden and the human relationship with God.

Catholic scholars recognise that the Genesis creation accounts are primarily theological texts, not scientific reports. They communicate truths about who God is (Creator, good, personal), who humanity is (made in the image of God, called to relationship and responsibility), and what went wrong (the Fall, Original Sin). These truths remain authoritative for Catholics regardless of how the physical universe came into being.

Genesis 1:26–27 is the crucial text: “Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness” — establishing the imago Dei (image of God). Catholic theology has reflected on this for centuries. St Augustine, St Thomas Aquinas and many others saw the imago Dei as humanity’s rational, moral and relational nature — the capacity to know God, to choose good and to love.

Not all Christians interpret Genesis the same way. Literalists (sometimes called young-earth creationists) hold that Genesis 1 is a straightforward historical account: the world was created in six twenty-four-hour days, a view sometimes associated with certain evangelical Protestant communities. They argue Scripture must be taken at face value on all matters, including the age and origins of the earth.

Day-age theorists propose that the six “days” of Genesis 1 correspond to long epochs of time. This allows a broad compatibility with the scientific account of deep time while retaining a sequential creation narrative. Other Christians, including many Catholics, embrace theistic evolution: God created the universe and set natural processes in motion through which all life, including humanity, developed. God’s special creative action is seen in the gift of a rational and moral soul, not in bypassing natural processes. Pope John Paul II in a 1996 address to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences affirmed that evolution is “more than just a hypothesis” and is compatible with Catholic faith, provided that the spiritual soul is seen as directly created by God.

Sacred Art: Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam

One of the most famous images in the history of art, Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam (c.1508–1512) forms part of the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican. The fresco depicts the moment from Genesis 1:26–27 when God breathes life into the first human. God reaches across the void towards Adam, whose arm is extended in a mirror image — two hands almost touching. The gap between the fingertips has been interpreted as the space between the divine and the human, bridged by God’s initiative.

Theologically, the painting communicates core Catholic doctrines: God is personal (depicted in human-like form to make the divine act comprehensible), creation is an act of love and gift, and human beings are made in the imago Dei — called into relationship with their Creator. The work is not merely beautiful; it is catechetical — it teaches doctrine visually at a time when most worshippers could not read. The Sistine Chapel as a whole was designed for the conclave in which the Pope is elected: every surface reinforces Catholic faith in a visual theology.

Key Fact

Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam depicts Genesis 1:26–27 visually — God reaching across the void to give life to Adam. It communicates the imago Dei (humanity made in God’s image), the personal nature of God and the Catholic belief that human life is a divine gift. It is housed in the Sistine Chapel, Vatican City.

The Tree of Life Mosaic at San Clemente, Rome

The apse mosaic of the Basilica of San Clemente in Rome (twelfth century) presents a complex symbolic programme drawing together themes of creation, salvation and the Church. At the centre of the mosaic is the Cross of Christ, but the cross is also depicted as a Tree of Life — a reference that connects it to the tree in the Garden of Eden (Genesis 2–3) and to the tree of life described in the book of Revelation (22:2). This connection suggests that Christ’s Cross restores what was lost at the Fall: access to God and to eternal life.

From the cross-tree spread vines, tendrils and leaves, filling the apse with abundant imagery of growth and life. Within the imagery appear the symbols of the four Evangelists — the winged man (Matthew), the lion (Mark), the ox (Luke) and the eagle (John) — proclaiming that the Gospels carry the life of the Tree to the world. The dove — symbol of the Holy Spirit — appears above or near the cross. The mosaic thus presents a compressed vision of Catholic belief: the Trinity, the Incarnation, the Cross as salvation, the Scriptures and the Church all intertwined in one visual whole.

Catholic theology frequently describes Jesus as the New Adam. The idea comes from St Paul’s letter to the Romans (5:12–21) and 1 Corinthians (15:21–22): just as through one man (Adam) sin and death entered the world, so through one man (Christ) come grace and life. The San Clemente mosaic embodies this by placing the cross (the instrument of Christ’s death and resurrection) in the position of the Tree of Life — visually declaring that Christ as New Adam restores humanity’s access to God.

The Alpha and Omega symbols often appear near the cross in Byzantine and Romanesque art, reinforcing the theological claim that Christ is himself the beginning and end of all things — the one in whom creation finds its meaning and destiny. The Chi-Rho also frequently appears in early Christian art to identify the figure on the cross or in the apse as the Christ, Lord of all.

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Creation of Adam by Michelangelo communicates about Catholic beliefs.

practice_questions.text: Explain the influence of the Catholic understanding of literary forms on how Catholics read Genesis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that recognising literary forms means Genesis 1 is read as a theological poem (not a science textbook); the seven-day structure is a liturgical framework; the truth communicated is about God as Creator, human dignity (imago Dei) and the Fall — not the physical mechanism of creation. Influences Catholic acceptance of theistic evolution. Reference to Dei Verbum or the Catechism. Secure: Two developed points of influence. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two different Christian views on the Genesis accounts of creation.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two contrasting views, each developed with a source. View 1: Literalist — Genesis 1 is a straightforward historical record; the world was created in six twenty-four-hour days; Scripture must be taken at face value on all matters; basis in a reading of Genesis 1:1–2:3 as historical narrative. View 2: Theistic evolution — God created through natural processes; Catholics (including Pope John Paul II's 1996 Pontifical Academy address) affirm evolution is compatible with faith provided the rational soul is directly created by God; Genesis is theological, not scientific. Each view explained with reasoning and source. Secure: Two views with one source. Developing: One view developed. Emerging: Simple statement of one view.

practice_questions.text:
'Sacred art is more important than Scripture for understanding Catholic beliefs.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Sacred art (e.g. Creation of Adam, San Clemente mosaic) communicates complex doctrine visually and accessibly — before widespread literacy, art was the primary means by which ordinary Catholics learned theology. Art can make abstract doctrines (imago Dei, Trinity, salvation) emotionally vivid. Art is less open to misinterpretation through language barriers. Arguments against: Scripture is the Word of God — divinely inspired, authoritative and the foundation of all Catholic doctrine. The Catechism, Dei Verbum and tradition all give Scripture primacy as a source of revelation. Art interprets Scripture; it cannot replace it. Theological meaning in art depends on the viewer knowing the Scriptural narrative behind it. Non-religious view: Both Scripture and art are human creations reflecting human culture and experience; neither is uniquely authoritative. Conclusion: A strong answer will argue that art and Scripture are complementary rather than competing — art embodies and extends Scriptural truth. Most Catholics would hold Scripture as primary while valuing art as a vital mode of theological expression. Mastering: Sustained argument, sources named and interpreted, justified conclusion. Secure: Two sides with one source. Developing: One side. Emerging: Simple statement.

lessons.title: Loving and Serving: Catholic Social Teaching in Britain

before.content_html:
Imago Dei as the Foundation of Catholic Social Teaching

The Catholic understanding of what it means to love and serve others begins with a single conviction: every human being is made in the image of God — the imago Dei. Because human dignity is God-given, not earned or granted by governments, it cannot be stripped away. This conviction shapes the whole tradition of Catholic Social Teaching (CST), which has developed over more than a century of papal encyclicals and Church documents.

The Second Vatican Council’s Gaudium et Spes (“Joy and Hope”, 1965) is one of the most important documents in this tradition. Paragraph 29 teaches that all human beings possess the same dignity regardless of race, sex, social condition or religion, because all are made in God’s image. Paragraph 78 connects this dignity to the call for justice, peace and reconciliation: the Church’s mission is not only spiritual but also social — to transform the structures of society so that they reflect the dignity of every person.

Key Fact

Gaudium et Spes (Second Vatican Council, 1965) at paragraph 29 teaches that all people share equal dignity because all are made in the image of God. Paragraph 78 links this dignity to the Church’s work for justice, peace and reconciliation in society.

The Principles of Catholic Social Teaching

Catholic Social Teaching rests on several interlocking principles. Human dignity is the foundation: every person deserves respect because they bear the image of God. The common good means that society must be organised so that everyone can flourish — not just the wealthy or powerful. Solidarity calls Catholics to see themselves as members of one human family and to stand with those who suffer. Subsidiarity means that decisions should be taken at the most local level possible, with higher authorities supporting rather than overriding local communities. Care for creation recognises that the earth is a gift from God to be stewarded, not exploited — a theme developed especially in Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015).

These principles are not abstract theories. They have generated a rich tradition of Catholic activism: trade unions, schools, hospitals, credit unions, housing associations and international development organisations. The call to love one’s neighbour (Luke 10:25–37, the parable of the Good Samaritan) is understood as demanding concrete social action, not merely private kindness.

Genesis 1:28 gives humanity dominion over the earth, but Catholic Social Teaching insists this is stewardship, not ownership. God declared creation “very good” (Genesis 1:31) and entrusted it to human care. Pope Francis’s Laudato Si’ (2015) extended Catholic Social Teaching explicitly to the environment — arguing that care for the poor and care for the earth are inseparable. The encyclical calls for an “ecological conversion”: a change of heart that sees the planet as a shared home entrusted to all of humanity, not a resource to be consumed.

This ecological dimension reflects a deeper point: CST is not just about human-to-human justice. It sees all created reality as caught up in God’s purposes. Catholics are called to respect creation as an expression of respect for its Creator and for future generations who will inherit the earth.

CAFOD: Catholic Action for Development

CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) is the official aid and development agency of the Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales. Founded in 1962, CAFOD works in over 40 countries worldwide, addressing poverty, hunger, displacement and injustice. Its work is explicitly grounded in Catholic Social Teaching — the belief that poverty is not just a practical problem but a moral one, since it violates the dignity of people made in God’s image.

CAFOD operates through local partners in the communities it serves, embodying the principle of subsidiarity. It campaigns for systemic change as well as delivering emergency aid: poverty is not just about immediate suffering but about unjust structures that keep people poor. Catholics in Britain support CAFOD through parish fundraising, Fast Days (giving up a meal and donating the money) and advocacy campaigns. CAFOD works alongside other aid organisations while maintaining its Catholic identity and theological motivation.

Key Fact

CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) was founded in 1962 and is the official Catholic development charity of England and Wales. It works in over 40 countries, motivated by the Catholic Social Teaching principle that every person’s dignity must be respected and that poverty is a moral injustice, not merely a practical problem.

The St Vincent de Paul Society: Local Charity

While CAFOD operates internationally, the St Vincent de Paul Society (SVP) focuses on local, face-to-face service. Founded in Paris in 1833 by a group of students inspired by the model of the seventeenth-century saint Vincent de Paul, the SVP now operates in over 150 countries. In Britain, SVP members visit those who are lonely or housebound, support people in poverty and crisis, and run food banks, prison visiting programmes and holiday schemes for children in deprived areas.

The SVP embodies the principle of solidarity: its members do not simply write cheques but enter into personal friendship with those they serve. The model is the Good Samaritan — not merely providing material help but accompanying the person in need. The SVP understands its work as part of what the Catechism calls the corporal works of mercy (feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick and imprisoned), rooted in Matthew 25:31–46, where Jesus identifies himself with the poor and vulnerable.

The Catholic Church’s commitment to inter-faith dialogue grew significantly through the Second Vatican Council. The declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) acknowledged the truth and goodness found in other religious traditions — in Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism and others — while insisting that Christ is the fullness of God’s revelation. The Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions.

In Britain, the Catholic Bishops’ Conference maintains inter-faith advisers who facilitate dialogue with Muslim, Jewish, Hindu, Sikh and Buddhist communities. Bodies such as the Council of Christians and Jews and the Christian-Muslim Forum bring religious communities together to address shared concerns: social justice, religious freedom and community cohesion. This engagement reflects the conviction that the imago Dei is found in every human being, regardless of their religion, and that working together for the common good is itself an expression of love for one’s neighbour. Britain’s own diversity of religious traditions — Christianity in its many denominations, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism — makes inter-faith dialogue not an abstract ideal but a daily necessity in parish and school life.
before.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about CAFOD or the SVP, don’t just describe what they do — explain why they do it, linking their work to a specific teaching (imago Dei, Gaudium et Spes 29, the Good Samaritan, Matthew 25). Examiners consistently reward candidates who connect practice to theology rather than giving a purely factual account. For 15-mark questions on social justice, use the principle of imago Dei as your anchor: if every person bears God’s image, social injustice is a theological offence, not just a social problem.

practice_questions.text: Give two principles of Catholic Social Teaching.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two: human dignity; the common good; solidarity; subsidiarity; care for creation; preferential option for the poor. Two marks maximum.

practice_questions.text: What does the term 'Catholic Social Teaching' mean?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The body of Catholic teaching on the moral dimensions of economic, political and social life, rooted in the God-given dignity of every person and including principles such as the common good, solidarity and subsidiarity. Secure: Catholic teaching about justice, poverty and human dignity. Developing: The Church's teaching about helping others. Emerging: What Catholics believe about society.

practice_questions.text: Describe the work of CAFOD and explain how it is motivated by Catholic Social Teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Accurate description of CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development, official charity of Bishops' Conference of England and Wales, founded 1962, works in over 40 countries); explains what it does (emergency aid, development work, advocacy, Fast Days); links explicitly to CST — imago Dei means poverty is a moral injustice; mentions subsidiarity (working through local partners); or Gaudium et Spes 29. Secure: Accurate description with two features and one CST link. Developing: Some accurate content about CAFOD with basic CST mention. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain the influence of the parable of the Good Samaritan on Catholic charity work in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the parable (Luke 10:25–37 — Samaritan crosses boundaries to help a stranger); influence: models neighbour-love as crossing social/religious boundaries; motivates both CAFOD (reaching across global barriers) and SVP (personal presence with those in need, not just financial help); connects to Matthew 25:31–46 (serving Christ in the poor). Secure: Two developed points of influence. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the Catholic belief in imago Dei shapes Catholic attitudes towards other religions.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Catholic belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed ways with sources. Way 1: Imago Dei means every person — regardless of religion — has inherent dignity and deserves respect; this grounds inter-faith dialogue; Nostra Aetate (1965) acknowledged truth and goodness in other religions (Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism). Way 2: Working with people of other faiths for the common good is itself an expression of love for God's image in the neighbour; the SVP and CAFOD work alongside non-Catholic partners. Each way with source and interpretation. Secure: Two ways with one source. Developing: One developed way. Emerging: Simple statement.

'Giving to charity is more important than working for structural change in society.'
Evaluate this statement from a Catholic perspective. In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching

• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Immediate charity relieves urgent suffering — SVP visiting the housebound, CAFOD delivering emergency aid. The corporal works of mercy (Matthew 25:31–46) focus on concrete acts of kindness. Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan shows direct personal help. Faith without works is dead (James 2:17). Arguments against: Catholic Social Teaching distinguishes between charity (addressing symptoms) and justice (addressing causes). Gaudium et Spes 29 and 78 call for transformation of social structures that violate human dignity. CAFOD campaigns for systemic change (debt relief, fair trade) alongside aid. Giving charity without challenging unjust structures can perpetuate the problem. Structural sin — the concept that unjust systems are themselves sinful — demands structural solutions. Non-religious view: Humanists would agree that systemic injustice must be addressed but might question whether religious motivation changes the nature of the action. Conclusion: A strong answer will argue that Catholic teaching holds both in tension — immediate charity is essential, but justice demands structural change. Mastering: Sustained two-sided argument, sources interpreted, clear conclusion. Secure: Two sides, one source. Developing: One side. Emerging: Simple view.
